fields.key: #wrap_element_operation_report > div.card-body > div:nth-child(3) > div > div > div.note-editing-area > div.note-editable.card-block
fields.value: Topical/local anesthesia → sterile preparation and draping → corneal main & side-port incisions → injection of viscoelastic (OVD) → continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (CCC) → hydrodissection & hydrodelineation → phacoemulsification of lens nucleus → cortical aspiration (I/A) → capsular bag inflation with OVD → foldable Intraocular Lens implantation → Intraocular Lens positioning & centration → removal of residual OVD → hydration/sealing of corneal wounds → intracameral antibiotic (if indicated) → eye patch/shield.

fields.key: #wrap_element_operation_report > div.card-body > div:nth-child(3) > div > div > div.note-editing-area > div.note-editable.card-block
fields.value: Topical/local anesthesia → sterile preparation and draping → pterygium head dissection from the cornea → excision of pterygium body and Tenon's tissue → smoothing of corneal surface → measurement of bare scleral defect → harvesting conjunctival autograft → graft orientation and placement (limbus-to-limbus) → graft fixation (fibrin glue or sutures) → wound inspection and hemostasis → topical antibiotic/steroid → eye patch/shield.

Redness, irritation, and a "growth" on the white of the eye
History: Significant UV/sun exposure, wind, or dust. 
No history of ocular trauma.

Conjunctiva: Triangular, vascularized wedge of conjunctival tissue extending from the nasal bulbar conjunctiva onto the cornea
Cornea: Pterygium apex extends 3mm past the limbus onto the cornea. No underlying infiltration or severe thinning.
Anterior Chamber: Deep and quiet, no cell/flare.
Tear Film: Intermittent localized drying/staining at the advancing head of the pterygium
Return 3 to 6 months for monitoring, or sooner if rapid growth or vision changes occur

Protection: Strict UV protection counseling (wraparound sunglasses, wide-brimmed hats outdoors).
Lubrication: 4 times a day or as needed
Anti-inflammatory Medication: To reduce the conjunctival inflammation
Monitor progression of cornea encroachment
Patient complain of irritation and foreign body sensation after cataract surgery on both eye

Conjunctiva: Mild injection
Cornea: Clear, no endothelial decompensation or surgical edema.
Anterior Chamber: Deep and quiet, no 
Iris: Round, reactive, no transillumination defects or synechiae
Lens (IOL): Pseudophakic. IOL is well-centered and stable within the capsular bag.
Presence of Intraocular Lens, Bilateral (Z96.1): Stable pseudophakia bilaterally, clear visual axis, well-positioned implants.
Recheck visual acuity, posterior capsule status and Intraocular lens stability , and follow up 1 year for routine wellness, or PRN.

Monitoring: Annual comprehensive eye examination to track IOL stability, capsular clarity, and long-term retinal health.
Patient Education: Advise on symptoms of delayed complications, specifically PCO (gradual blur) and retinal detachment (flashes, showers of floaters, curtain over vision). Instruct to return immediately if noted.
Lubrication eye drop for dry eye related symptom
Mild steroid eye drop for mild inflammation
Follow UP: 1 year for routine wellness, or PRN.
Redness, discharge, and irritation in both eye

Lids/Lashes: Mild edema / Matte purulent discharge on lashes
Conjunctiva: Moderate bulbar and palpebral injection. Palpebral conjunctiva reveals Diffuse papillae. No pseudomembranes present.
Cornea: Clear, compact, negative fluorescein staining. No subepithelial infiltrates or dendrites.
Anterior Chamber: Deep and quiet; no cell or flare.
Follow up 3 to 5 days if no improvement, or immediately if visual acuity drops, severe photophobia develops, or pain worsens.

Therapeutics (Bacterial): use Ofloxacin 0.3% or Tobramycin 0.3% QID
Topical steroid to hazen the recovery of the inflammation.
Supportive care: artificial tears and cool compresses QID. 
Strict hygiene/handwashing education to prevent cross-contamination
Discontinuation: Suspend all contact lens wear and discard active lenses/cases if infectious.

Gradual, progressive blurring of vision bilaterally for the past several months.
Pertinent History: No history of ocular trauma, prolonged topical steroid use, or poorly controlled diabetes. Intermittent outdoor UV exposure without protection.

Refraction: Manifest shows a myopic shift (secondary to nuclear sclerosis).
Cornea: Clear, normal endothelial luster, no guttae.
Anterior Chamber: Deep and quiet, no cell/flare.
Lens: dense Nuclear Sclerosis (NS) bilaterally.
Fundus (Dilated): Lens opacity limits view, but optic nerve appears intact with a C/D ratio of 0.5 Both eye. Macula flat, gross vasculature stable. No obvious peripheral pathology.
Follow up for change in visual acuity, intraocular pressure, lens progression or when patient decide to undergo cataract surgery.

Conservative Management: Updated spectacle prescription issued today to maximize current visual potential. 
Surgical Discussion: Discussed risks, benefits, and alternatives of phacoemulsification with IOL implantation.
